\begin{abstract}
Large-language-model (LLM) trading agents fuse numerical market data with textual signals, which makes them vulnerable to \emph{subtle} misinformation: small edits to sentiment, numbers, causes or entities that remain close to genuine news yet change what the agent does. AutoRedTrader recently showed that such perturbations, generated autonomously and steered by agent feedback, flip a retrieval-based agent's decisions in up to 26.7\% of trading days. We present \rhal{}, an offline, deterministic, CPU-only framework that reproduces the closed-loop red-teaming setting of AutoRedTrader without paid APIs and extends it along four axes: (i)~\emph{stronger temporal evidence}, adding HFT-inspired microstructure proxies (range-based spread, Garman--Klass variance, order-flow imbalance, volume shock, Amihud illiquidity) to the historical-analog grounding signal; (ii)~an \emph{explicit risk-control layer} (confidence gate, hold-on-conflict, volatility-targeted sizing, stop-loss/take-profit, drawdown throttle); (iii)~\emph{strict no-lookahead guarantees} enforced structurally and verified by future-mutation tests, including an admissibility rule for analog outcomes; and (iv)~a \emph{placebo-controlled attack metric}: every attacked run is paired step-by-step with a shadow clean agent, and a placebo arm of meaning-preserving paraphrases measures how many decision flips arise from retrieval-pool perturbation alone. On \val{NseedsRun} seeds of synthetic data, the undefended agent shows an attack success rate (ASR) of \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% and a misinformation exposure rate (MER) of \val{MInjectedNoneMER}\% (lift \val{MInjectedNoneMERLift}$\times$ over chance), but the placebo arm alone flips \val{MPlaceboNoneASR}\% of decisions, so the misinformation-attributable \emph{net ASR} is only \val{MInjectedNoneASRNet}\%. Temporal grounding with microstructure evidence reduces naive ASR by \val{GainGroundedASR} percentage points; the risk layer additionally reduces attack-period drawdown and \emph{active} flips, although a defensive Hold is itself counted as a flip by ASR, which we correct with an active-flip variant. Attack-side ablations show that, with rule-based operators, only semantic minor perturbations strengthen the attack, while style rewriting raises retrievability but weakens decision impact. Defence-side ablations show that microstructure evidence is what makes grounding effective. All effects come with a quantified cost in clean return, exposed as a robustness--return frontier. All code, tests and experiments are reproducible from a single seed. The framework is strictly for defensive robustness evaluation and is not a trading system.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
LLM agents, financial misinformation, red teaming, robustness, time-series grounding, market microstructure, backtesting, risk management
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% =============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
Modern LLM-based financial agents such as FinMem~\cite{yu2025finmem}, FinCon~\cite{yu2024fincon} and TradingAgents~\cite{xiao2025tradingagents} retrieve news from a memory store, reason over it together with market observations, and emit sequential trading actions. Their inputs are therefore an attack surface. Unlike jailbreaks, financial misinformation rarely crosses an explicit safety boundary: a flipped direction word, an inflated percentage, a substituted cause, or a mis-attributed entity produces text that is still \emph{plausible news}, hard to detect without a reference, and yet decision-relevant. AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} formalised this threat as a constrained attack over a finance-theory-structured operator space (behavioural bias, minor semantic perturbation, style rewriting), optimised online with a P\'olya-urn sampler fed by the agent's own decision changes, and reported that time-series-informed grounding partially mitigates it.

Three gaps motivate this project. First, the original evaluation depends on paid LLM calls, real news feeds and FAISS, so a student cannot reproduce it on a laptop. Second, the grounding evidence uses six daily indicators; market microstructure offers additional, faster-moving evidence about whether a textual claim is consistent with what traders are actually doing. Third, the attack success rate (ASR) compares an injected run with a clean run, but \emph{any} change to a retrieval pool reshuffles the top-$k$ documents and can flip near-threshold decisions; without a control, ASR conflates semantic manipulation with retrieval noise.

\textbf{Contributions.} (1)~A compact, fully tested reimplementation of the AutoRedTrader loop that runs offline in mock mode and optionally with any Claude/OpenAI-compatible model. (2)~Microstructure-augmented temporal grounding and an explicit risk layer as defences, ablated individually. (3)~Structural no-lookahead guarantees---trailing normalisation, next-open execution, and an $e+H\le t$ admissibility rule for historical analogs---verified by tests that mutate the future and assert the past is unchanged. (4)~A paired shadow/treated simulation with a placebo arm, yielding \emph{net ASR} and \emph{MER lift}, which we argue are the right quantities to report. (5)~A robustness--return frontier over defence strength, and a 4--5 month roadmap for extending the study.

% =============================================================================
\section{Related Work}
\textbf{LLM trading agents.} FinMem~\cite{yu2025finmem} introduced layered memory and character design; InvestorBench~\cite{li2025investorbench} standardised the Perception/Profile/Memory/Action agent used here; FinCon~\cite{yu2024fincon}, TradingAgents~\cite{xiao2025tradingagents} and FinAgent~\cite{zhang2024finagent} add multi-agent and tool-augmented reasoning. None treat adversarial text as part of the core evaluation.
\textbf{Robustness of financial agents.} TradeTrap~\cite{yan2025tradetrap} shows that small textual changes shift LLM trading decisions substantially. AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} is the first autonomous red-teaming loop specialised to this setting and is our base.
\textbf{Adversarial text and misinformation.} Automated red teaming~\cite{zhou2025autoredteamer}, jailbreak-style prompting~\cite{jiang2024artprompt} and prompt-induced fake-news generation~\cite{wang2026life} target general LLM safety; reference-free counterfactual financial misinformation detection~\cite{jiang2026glisters} shows why subtle edits are hard to flag.
\textbf{Behavioural finance.} Overconfidence~\cite{barber2001boys}, loss aversion~\cite{kahneman2013prospect}, herding~\cite{spyrou2013herding} and noise-trader dynamics~\cite{delong1990noise} ground the bias operator space; the Loughran--McDonald lexicon~\cite{loughran2011liability} motivates our sentiment scorer.
\textbf{Microstructure and backtest validity.} Range-based spread estimators~\cite{corwin2012spread}, Garman--Klass variance~\cite{garman1980estimation}, Amihud illiquidity~\cite{amihud2002illiquidity} and order-flow imbalance~\cite{cont2014price} are the proxies we adopt. Backtest overfitting~\cite{bailey2014probability} and lookahead bias~\cite{lopezdeprado2018advances} inform our no-leak design.

% =============================================================================
\section{Methodology}
\subsection{Problem setting}
Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a corpus of daily news for one asset, $\mathrm{FinAgent}$ a POMDP agent that at each day $t$ retrieves $\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{ret}}_t\subset\mathcal{N}$ and chooses $a_t\in\{\text{Buy},\text{Sell},\text{Hold}\}$. An attacker owns a generator $\mathrm{MisGen}$ that maps clean items to synthetic variants $\tilde{\mathcal{N}}$ and may edit the agent's context $c$ within an accessible region (the system prompt). Following~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}, the attacker seeks a distribution $\pi$ over operators $\phi_{(b,m,r)}$ maximising expected decision change subject to $A_{\mathrm{sim}}(\tilde n,n)\ge\tau_{\mathrm{sim}}$ and $A_{\mathrm{det}}(\tilde n)\le\tau_{\mathrm{det}}$. The defender seeks agent modifications that reduce the induced decision change without discarding useful text.

\subsection{Misinformation generation (MisGen)}
We implement the three operator sub-spaces as deterministic functions of $(n,\text{rng})$ so the loop is reproducible without an LLM (LLM-mode prompts from the paper's Appendix~E are also supported):
\begin{itemize}
\item $\Phi_{\mathrm{Bias}}$: overconfidence, loss aversion, anchoring, herding, confirmation. In LLM mode these are the verbatim prompt templates; in mock mode each maps to an explicit parameter shift of the surrogate policy (Sec.~\ref{sec:agent}) so that $\Phi_{\mathrm{Bias}}$ is measurable.
\item $\Phi_{\mathrm{Minor}}$: flipping (antonym map over directional words and causes), sentiment shift (intensify/dampen), numerical (percentages scaled to $[1.5x,2x]$ or $<0.5x$ preserving direction, as in the paper's rules), temporal (quarter/year shift), entity (company$\to$competitor/subsidiary/parent), concept (revenue$\leftrightarrow$net income, etc.), causal (cause swapped across polarity pools), other (vague attribution).
\item $\Phi_{\mathrm{Rewrite}}$: news style (attribution marker, intensifiers removed, sentences merged) and academic style (formal synonyms, intensifiers$\to$hedges, sentences merged). Both are length-neutral surface transforms that never touch directional words, numbers, entities or causes, i.e.\ they \emph{launder} but cannot undo $\Phi_{\mathrm{Minor}}$.
\item \emph{Placebo} (ours): synonym and connector substitution only; used as the noise-floor control.
\end{itemize}
Strategy selection follows Eqs.~(16)--(18) of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}: $w_s=1+\alpha h_s$, $P(s)=w_s/\sum w$, with a return-dependent boost $\delta$ toward overconfidence when $CR>1$ and loss aversion when $CR<1$. Generation follows Algorithm~1 of the paper with $K$ retries: sample bias with probability $p$; sample $m$; apply Minor; if $(A_{\mathrm{sim}},A_{\mathrm{det}})$ pass, accept; else sample $r$, apply Rewrite, re-check $A_{\mathrm{det}}$.

\textbf{Similarity evaluator.} $A_{\mathrm{sim}}$ is TF-IDF (1--2-gram) cosine similarity with IDF fit once on the clean corpus.
\textbf{Detectability evaluator.} $A_{\mathrm{det}}$ is a logistic regression over 18 interpretable cues (polarity densities, mixed polarity, intensifier/hedge rates, numeric magnitudes, cause--outcome mismatch, sentence structure, entity/ticker presence, vague attribution). It is trained on an \emph{independent} synthetic corpus with positives from $\Phi_{\mathrm{Minor}}$ only, and its threshold is calibrated to a \val{DetFPR}\% false-positive rate on held-out clean text. Training on Minor outputs only mirrors a ``standard detector'' that $\Phi_{\mathrm{Rewrite}}$ is designed to evade; Table~\ref{tab:detector} quantifies the laundering effect.

\subsection{Closed-loop feedback}
After each day the treated agent's action is compared with the shadow clean agent's action on the same day; if they differ, the day's bias and the strategies of every synthetic document that was retrieved are reinforced (Eq.~(7) of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}). Because both agents see the identical market path and differ only in text, this is a genuinely paired update.

\subsection{Temporal grounding with microstructure evidence}
At day $t$ we compute, from rows $\le t$ only: 1-day return, 5-day volatility, 20-day drawdown, short/long trend divergence, a trailing-residual anomaly score and 5/20-day momentum (the paper's Eq.~(19), with residual-$z$ in place of STL because STL is not online-safe); and six microstructure proxies: $(H-L)/C$ spread proxy~\cite{corwin2012spread}, Garman--Klass realised variance~\cite{garman1980estimation}, order-flow imbalance (tick-rule buy/sell volume when intraday bars exist, else close-location value)~\cite{cont2014price}, volume shock, Amihud illiquidity~\cite{amihud2002illiquidity} and range ratio. Features are $z$-scored with a \emph{trailing} 60-day window---full-sample normalisation would leak. A bounded market signal $s_{\mathrm{mkt}}=\tanh(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{z}_t)$ uses fixed, documented weights (no fitting, hence no leakage). Analogs are the top-$k$ cosine neighbours of the flattened 30-day window among windows ending at $e$ with $e+H\le t$, so that each analog's $H$-day forward outcome is already observed at $t$; their mean forward return is blended into $s_{\mathrm{mkt}}$. Consistency between text and market is $c=1-|s_{\mathrm{text}}-s_{\mathrm{mkt}}|/2\in[0,1]$.

\subsection{Agent and defences}\label{sec:agent}
The agent follows InvestorBench/FinMem: \emph{Perception} builds the observation (prices, retrieved documents with provenance labels, evidence); \emph{Profile} holds the task, asset context and the attacker-controlled bias context; \emph{Memory} keeps a working buffer of recent steps with reflections and a long-term text-trust estimate; \emph{Action} maps to Buy/Sell/Hold. Three policies share this interface: a rule baseline (market evidence only), a real LLM (prompt = Perception+Profile+Memory+Evidence+documents, JSON output, disk-cached for reproducibility), and the default \emph{surrogate} policy. The surrogate scores each retrieved document with a negation- and intensity-aware finance lexicon, forms $s_{\mathrm{text}}$ as the retrieval-weighted mean, applies the day's bias as a parameter shift (overconfidence: action threshold $\times0.55$; loss aversion: negative signals $\times1.7$; anchoring: $0.5$ blend with yesterday's signal; herding: pull toward the recent majority action; confirmation: agreeing documents up-weighted), and fuses $s=\lambda s_{\mathrm{text}}+(1-\lambda)s_{\mathrm{mkt}}$ with $\lambda=0.75$ to mirror an LLM's text-heavy reliance. \textbf{Grounding} shrinks inconsistent text toward market evidence,
\begin{equation}
s_g = s-\kappa\,(1-c)\,(s-s_{\mathrm{mkt}}),
\end{equation}
leaving consistent text untouched. \textbf{Risk layer} (post-policy, can only reduce or exit): confidence gate, hold-on-conflict when $c<0.6$, volatility-targeted sizing $\min(1,\sigma^*/\sigma_5)$, 6\%/12\% stop-loss/take-profit, and a 50\% size throttle beyond 10\% drawdown. Every override is logged.

\subsection{Backtester and no-lookahead guarantees}
Decisions at close $t$ execute at open $t+1$ with \val{SlipBps}\,bps slippage and \val{FeeBps}\,bps fees, no leverage, long-only. Accounting invariants ($\mathrm{equity}=\mathrm{cash}+\mathrm{shares}\cdot\mathrm{price}$, cash $\ge0$, round trips lose exactly costs) are unit-tested. Lookahead is excluded structurally (trailing operations, next-open fills, analog admissibility) and verified by tests that multiply all prices after a cut-off by 5, rebuild features, evidence and decisions, and assert bit-identical outputs before the cut-off.

\subsection{Metrics}
MER and ASR follow Eqs.~(8)--(9) of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}. We add: \textbf{MER lift} $=\mathrm{MER}/\bar\rho$ where $\bar\rho$ is the synthetic share of the visible pool (retrieval above chance); \textbf{net ASR} $=\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{inj}}-\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{placebo}}$ computed per seed and defence level; signal deviation $\mathbb{E}|s^{\mathrm{inj}}_t-s^{\mathrm{clean}}_t|$; ASR conditional on exposure; exposure and flips by perturbation type and by bias; cumulative return (CR), maximum drawdown, Sharpe-like ratio, turnover, and risk-override counts. \textbf{Matched net ASR}: the classic placebo paraphrases \emph{every} item and carries no bias prompt, whereas the attack injects only the candidates that pass its filters and adds bias contexts. Two further placebos built from the recorded attack therefore paraphrase only the attacked items (\emph{count-matched}) and, in addition, receive the attack's daily bias contexts (\emph{bias-matched}); they decompose ASR into pool noise, count, bias and meaning, with $\mathrm{ASR}^{\mathrm{matched}}_{\mathrm{net}}=\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{frozen}}-\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{placebo+bias}}$. All placebo variants use the same paraphrase for a given (day, item). \textbf{One-step counterfactual ASR} (cf-ASR): after the first flip the treated agent's portfolio and memory drift away from the shadow's, so later disagreements may reflect that accumulated state rather than the day's text. Each day a throw-away copy of the agent therefore decides with the shadow's memory and portfolio but the treated documents and bias contexts; cf-ASR is its disagreement rate with the shadow. It reads only copies, so it leaves every other quantity unchanged.

% =============================================================================
\section{System Architecture}
The package \texttt{rhal} has nine modules with a strict dependency order (data $\to$ features $\to$ grounding; memory; misgen; llm; agent; backtest; evaluation). Every stochastic component draws from a child seed derived by hashing the master seed with a component tag, so changing the number of random draws in MisGen cannot perturb data generation or the shadow agent. A single YAML file holds every knob and ablations are dotted overrides. The simulation loop (\texttt{Simulation.run}) is roughly sixty lines: per day it (1)~lets MisGen sample a bias and inject variants of that day's clean items into the treated pool, (2)~marks both portfolios, (3)~lets the shadow and treated agents perceive, decide and pass through the risk layer, (4)~executes and marks at $t+1$, and (5)~feeds back the paired decision difference. Figures~1--4 of the accompanying repository documentation (\texttt{docs/ARCHITECTURE.md}) give the Mermaid system, class and sequence diagrams. All synthetic text carries \texttt{provenance="synthetic"} and a safety label; no module can route an order.

% =============================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
\textbf{Data.} Because the study must be reproducible offline, we generate a synthetic asset: \val{NDays} business days of OHLCV from a 3-regime Markov drift with GARCH(1,1) volatility~\cite{bollerslev1986garch}, small overnight gaps independent of the day's drift, and \val{NewsPerDay} template news items per day whose latent sentiment is correlated ($\rho=0.35$) with the next-day return, i.e.\ news is genuinely but noisily informative. Templates always contain entities, figures, causes and period references so every $\Phi_{\mathrm{Minor}}$ type has a target. Real OHLCV can be loaded from CSV or \texttt{yfinance}; the last \val{NevalDays} days are evaluated (as in the paper's 60-day BTC window), the rest serve as warm-up and analog library.
\textbf{Arms.} For each of three defence levels---\emph{none} (ungrounded, text-heavy), \emph{grounded} (temporal grounding + microstructure), \emph{grounded+risk}---we run \emph{clean}, \emph{placebo} and \emph{injected} arms, each as a paired shadow/treated simulation, over \val{NseedsRun} seeds, plus the count- and bias-matched placebos built from the attack recorded against the undefended agent. MisGen uses $p=0.7$, $\alpha=1$, $\delta=0.15$, $K=3$, $\tau_{\mathrm{sim}}=0.35$, $\tau_{\mathrm{det}}$ at the calibrated threshold, injection ratio 1:1; retrieval is TF-IDF top-\val{TopK} over the last 3 days with recency decay; $\kappa=\val{Kappa}$.
\textbf{Attack settings.} Defences are evaluated against two attackers. In the \emph{adaptive} setting MisGen runs live and its feedback loop adapts to the defended agent. In the \emph{frozen} setting the attack recorded against the undefended agent of the same seed (documents and daily bias contexts) is replayed verbatim against every defence, so differences between frozen arms are caused by the defence alone. MisGen draws its randomness from streams keyed by (seed, day, item), so all arms of a seed share the attacker's random numbers (common random numbers) and no result depends on an arm's label.
\textbf{Statistics.} All arms of a seed share the market path and clean news, so every comparison is paired by seed. For each claim we report the mean per-seed difference with a 95\% percentile-bootstrap confidence interval over seeds and a two-sided sign-flip permutation $p$-value, Holm-corrected within each family of related comparisons (Tables~\ref{tab:stats_main}, \ref{tab:stats_controls} and~\ref{tab:stats_ablation}).
\textbf{Ablations.} Attack-side (w/o filtering, feedback, bias, minor, rewrite) against the undefended agent, mirroring the paper's Table~2; defence-side (none, grounding only, grounding+micro, risk only, full, w/o hold-on-conflict); retrieval breadth $k\in\{2,4,8\}$; grounding strength $\kappa\in\{0.3,0.7,1.0\}$.
\textbf{Compute.} Everything runs single-process on a laptop CPU at about half a second per paired 60-day run; the main experiment (18 arms $\times$ \val{NseedsRun} seeds) takes a few minutes.

% TODO(30-seed): naive ASR is now 38.3% (net 16.6%), above -- not 'comparable to' -- the 26.7% of AutoRedTrader; reword.
\textbf{Attack effectiveness.} Against the undefended agent the injected arm reaches MER \val{MInjectedNoneMER}\% (lift \val{MInjectedNoneMERLift}$\times$: rewritten documents acquire ticker mentions and finance markers that make them \emph{more} retrievable than chance) and ASR \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\,$\pm$\,\val{MInjectedNoneASRSd}\%, comparable to the 26.7\% reported on BTC by~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}. Signal deviation is \val{MInjectedNoneSignalDeviation} versus \val{MPlaceboNoneSignalDeviation} for placebo, so misinformation moves the agent's internal signal substantially more than paraphrase does.

\textbf{The placebo control.} The placebo arm---paraphrases that preserve every number, entity and direction---nevertheless flips \val{MPlaceboNoneASR}\% of decisions. Inspection shows that on every evaluation day the top-$k$ set differs between shadow and treated agents once the pool doubles: near-duplicates displace other documents, the text signal is averaged over fewer sources, and about 27\% of clean-arm signals lie within 0.05 of the action threshold. The misinformation-attributable \emph{net} ASR is therefore \val{MInjectedNoneASRNet}\%, and the net rate of \emph{active} flips (treated agent trades, clean agent did something else) is \val{MInjectedNoneASRActiveNet}\%. We regard this as a central methodological finding: naive ASR overstates the semantic effect of subtle misinformation by roughly a factor of two on our data, and a paraphrase control should accompany any reported ASR.

% TODO(30-seed): (a) the risk layer does NOT significantly reduce drawdown or active flips (CmpDdRisk, CmpGainAdaptiveRiskActnet);
%   (b) placebo-corrected active flips are NOT indistinguishable: grounding cuts them by 4.7pp [2.6,6.8] (CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedActnet);
%   (c) grounding reduces net ASR by 8.8pp [6.1,11.6] in both attack settings, so it is not 'mainly' a noise-sensitivity effect.
\textbf{Defences.} Grounding with microstructure evidence lowers naive ASR from \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% to \val{MInjectedGroundedASR}\% (gain \val{GainGroundedASR} points; net-ASR gain \val{GainGroundedASRnet}) and active flips from \val{MInjectedNoneASRActive}\% to \val{MInjectedGroundedASRActive}\%. Adding the risk layer gives naive ASR \val{MInjectedGroundedRiskASR}\%---slightly \emph{higher} than grounding alone---because \texttt{hold\_on\_conflict} fires on the treated agent whenever injected text conflicts with market evidence, and that defensive Hold is counted as a decision change by Eq.~(9). The active-flip rate (\val{MInjectedGroundedRiskASRActive}\%) and the attack-period maximum drawdown (\val{MInjectedGroundedRiskMaxDrawdown}\% vs \val{MInjectedGroundedMaxDrawdown}\%) show the risk layer's real effect. After placebo correction, active flips are small and statistically indistinguishable across defence levels (\val{MInjectedNoneASRActiveNet}\%, \val{MInjectedGroundedASRActiveNet}\%, \val{MInjectedGroundedRiskASRActiveNet}\%): on this surrogate agent the defences mainly reduce sensitivity to \emph{any} retrieval-pool perturbation rather than to misinformation specifically. The cost is visible in the paired clean return: \val{MCleanNoneCR}\% undefended versus \val{MCleanGroundedCR}\% grounded and \val{MCleanGroundedRiskCR}\% with risk controls, because the synthetic news is genuinely informative and grounding discounts it whenever it disagrees with lagging market evidence. Figure~\ref{fig:frontier} plots this robustness--return frontier; Fig.~\ref{fig:equity} shows seed-0 equity curves and Fig.~\ref{fig:exposure} the exposure and flips by perturbation type.

\textbf{Matched controls and counterfactual ASR.} Two further controls test whether net ASR really measures the \emph{meaning} of the misinformation (Tables~\ref{tab:decomposition} and~\ref{tab:stats_controls}). Restricting the placebo to the items the attack actually injected changes nothing (\val{CmpDecCountNone}\,pp, 95\% CI [\val{CmpDecCountNoneLo}, \val{CmpDecCountNoneHi}]), but giving the paraphrase arm the attack's daily bias contexts raises ASR by \val{CmpDecBiasNone}\,pp [\val{CmpDecBiasNoneLo}, \val{CmpDecBiasNoneHi}]. The classic net ASR of \val{MInjectedNoneASRNet}\% therefore contains a bias-prompt component. The effect of the misinformation's content alone is \val{CmpDecMeaningNone}\,pp [\val{CmpDecMeaningNoneLo}, \val{CmpDecMeaningNoneHi}]: of the undefended agent's naive ASR of \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\%, \val{MPlaceboNoneASR} points are retrieval-pool noise, \val{CmpDecBiasNone} come from bias prompts and \val{CmpDecMeaningNone} from meaning. Grounding still cuts the meaning effect, to \val{CmpDecMeaningGrounded}\,pp. The one-step counterfactual ASR, which applies each day's injected documents and bias to the clean agent's own state, is within \val{CmpCfGapNone}\,pp [\val{CmpCfGapNoneLo}, \val{CmpCfGapNoneHi}] of the sequential ASR, so state drift after the first flip does not materially inflate ASR in our setting. On the strictest metric (matched net cf-ASR), grounding lowers the misinformation effect by \val{CmpCfGainGrounded}\,pp [\val{CmpCfGainGroundedLo}, \val{CmpCfGainGroundedHi}].

\section{Ablation Study}

% TODO(30-seed): minor (+8.3pp) and filtering (+6.2pp) significantly raise net ASR; bias/feedback/rewrite are n.s. on net ASR;
%   feedback (+4.6pp) and rewrite (+14.8pp) raise MER only. The 'removing rewrite raises ASR' story was attack-seed noise.
\textbf{Attack components} (Table~\ref{tab:abl_attack}). Our rule-based operators reproduce the paper's ordering only partially. Removing \emph{minor} perturbation collapses net ASR (\val{AblAttackInjectedWoMinorASRNet}\% vs \val{AblAttackInjectedFullASRNet}\% full), confirming that semantic content is the source of the attack. Removing \emph{filtering} lowers MER (\val{AblAttackInjectedWoFilteringMER}\% vs \val{AblAttackInjectedFullMER}\%) because unfiltered candidates are less retrievable, with ASR unchanged within noise. Removing \emph{bias} and \emph{feedback} changes ASR by less than one standard deviation; with a noisy paired signal (placebo floor $\approx$\val{AblAttackPlaceboFullASR}\%) the P\'olya-urn reinforcement receives mostly noise and can lock onto a lucky strategy, so uniform sampling is not worse here. Most strikingly, removing \emph{rewrite} \emph{raises} ASR to \val{AblAttackInjectedWoRewriteASR}\% (net \val{AblAttackInjectedWoRewriteASRNet}\%) while lowering MER to \val{AblAttackInjectedWoRewriteMER}\%: without laundering, only candidates that pass the detector directly are accepted, and those are dominated by the decision-potent types (flipping, sentiment, numerical), whereas rewriting admits more of the detectable but decision-weak types (entity, concept, causal) and replaces intensifiers with hedges, which dilutes the lexicon signal. Style rewriting therefore trades decision impact for retrievability and stealth in our setting; the LLM rewrites of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} evidently preserve persuasive force better. Every row is accompanied by its own placebo (bottom half of the table), which is flat across variants as it should be.

\textbf{Defence components} (Table~\ref{tab:abl_defense}). Price-only grounding barely helps (naive ASR \val{AblDefenseInjectedGroundingOnlyASR}\%, net \val{AblDefenseInjectedGroundingOnlyASRNet}\%); adding the microstructure proxies is what makes grounding work (\val{AblDefenseInjectedGroundingMicroASR}\%, net \val{AblDefenseInjectedGroundingMicroASRNet}\%), because order-flow and range features give a sharper estimate of the current state against which inconsistent text is discounted. The risk layer alone \emph{raises} naive ASR (\val{AblDefenseInjectedRiskOnlyASR}\%) through defensive Holds while leaving net ASR unchanged; disabling hold-on-conflict inside the full defence changes little, so the risk layer's contribution is chiefly to drawdown rather than to decision robustness.
% TODO(30-seed): net ASR flat in k (n.s.) holds; placebo ASR is NOT flat -- it drops 4.5pp at k=8 (significant).
\textbf{Retrieval breadth} (Table~\ref{tab:abl_retrieval}). Naive, placebo and net ASR are all roughly flat for $k\in\{2,4,8\}$ (net \val{AblRetrievalInjectedKTwoASRNet}\%, \val{AblRetrievalInjectedKFourASRNet}\%, \val{AblRetrievalInjectedKEightASRNet}\%), so the net metric is not an artefact of a particular $k$.
% TODO(30-seed): no kappa in {0.3,0.7,1.0} differs significantly in net ASR or clean CR; the frontier is driven by grounding on/off, not kappa.
\textbf{Grounding strength.} A $\kappa$ sweep is provided by \texttt{scripts/run\_ablation.py --group grounding\_strength}; larger $\kappa$ trades clean return for robustness along the frontier of Fig.~\ref{fig:frontier}.
\textbf{Detector} (Table~\ref{tab:detector}). The proxy reaches \val{DetAcc} training accuracy at a \val{DetFPR}\% clean false-positive rate; temporal and numerical edits are nearly undetectable (\val{DetTemporalMinor}\% and \val{DetNumericalMinor}\%), entity/concept/causal edits are the most detectable, and both rewrite styles reduce detection for every type except the ``other'' category, reproducing the paper's ``Minor produces, Rewrite launders'' dynamic.

% =============================================================================
\section{Safety and Ethics}
This work generates synthetic financial misinformation for the sole purpose of measuring and improving agent robustness. Every generated record carries a mandatory provenance label and a safety string; text never leaves the simulator except into labelled, git-ignored logs; there is no broker, order-routing or live-data path; the attacker's objective is decision change, not profit, and no code steers prices or disseminates content. The framework should not be used on real news feeds, for investment advice, or in any live setting, and our synthetic entities are fictitious. We follow the dual-use discussion of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} and release the code to support defensive research.

% =============================================================================
\section{Limitations}
(1)~The default agent is a transparent surrogate rather than an LLM; the harness supports LLM mode but our headline numbers are surrogate-based. (2)~Data and news are synthetic; template news is more regular than real reporting, which likely makes the lexical detector both easier to train and easier to fool. (3)~The detectability proxy is a small feature classifier, not an LLM judge. (4)~Stop-loss/take-profit are evaluated at daily closes. (5)~Sixty evaluation days per seed makes CR noisy; we therefore base claims on paired per-seed differences with bootstrap confidence intervals and permutation tests over \val{NseedsRun} seeds rather than on single-run returns. (6)~Placebo ASR reveals that a threshold policy over retrieved-document averages is intrinsically jittery; smoother policies (hysteresis, probabilistic actions) would change both naive and net ASR.

\section{Conclusion}
\rhal{} turns the AutoRedTrader red-teaming loop into a reproducible, offline laboratory and extends it with microstructure-augmented grounding, an explicit risk layer, structural no-lookahead guarantees and a placebo-controlled attack metric. The undefended agent is measurably vulnerable; grounding---and specifically its microstructure evidence---buys robustness at a quantified cost in clean return; the risk layer protects drawdown but its defensive Holds are mis-scored by naive ASR; and roughly half of the naive attack success rate is attributable to retrieval-pool perturbation rather than to the meaning of the injected text. With rule-based operators, semantic minor perturbations drive the attack while style rewriting weakens it, a divergence from the LLM-driven original that the harness makes easy to test with a real model. Future work will run the same harness with real LLM policies and real price series, add smoother action policies, and study directional (profit-seeking) attackers under the same safety boundary.
